name: Gamepad Button & Input Tester
title: Gamepad Button and Input Tester | Toolkit Gen
description: Test gamepad buttons, analog stick deadzones, trigger travel, and polling rate in your browser with the Gamepad API.
author: ToolkitGen Engineering Team
quickAnswer: The Gamepad Button and Input Tester accesses connected controllers via the browser HTML5 Gamepad API without third-party drivers or software installations. It visualizes button actuation, analog trigger pressure from 0% to 100%, dual-stick Cartesian coordinates, and hardware USB or Bluetooth polling frequencies in real time. All processing runs locally in browser memory.
features: Full HTML5 Gamepad API Hardware Access
DualSense, Xbox, and Generic Controller Support
Analog Stick Coordinate Radar and Deadzone Verification

howTo.name: Connect Controller
howTo.text: Plug in your controller via USB or pair it over Bluetooth. Press any button on the gamepad to wake the browser interface.

howTo.name: Verify Device Detection
howTo.text: Confirm that your gamepad model name appears in the device status header.

howTo.name: Test Buttons and Triggers
howTo.text: Press each button, bumper, and analog trigger to confirm actuation and smooth analog value scaling from 0.00 to 1.00.

howTo.name: Inspect Analog Sticks
howTo.text: Move left and right thumbsticks to examine centering accuracy, deadzone threshold, and coordinate travel.

faq.q: Why is my controller not detected when I plug it in?
faq.a: Browsers enforce a security policy requiring a physical button press on the gamepad before exposing device input events to JavaScript. Connect the controller and press any button (such as A, Cross, or D-Pad) to activate detection.

Any controller recognized by your operating system as an XInput, DirectInput, or HID gamepad is supported, including PlayStation DualSense, DualShock 4, Xbox Wireless Controllers, Nintendo Switch Pro Controllers, and third-party fightsticks.

Polling rate is the frequency (measured in Hertz, or Hz) at which the controller transmits updated button and stick states to the host system. Standard Bluetooth connections typically poll between 125 Hz (8ms) and 250 Hz (4ms), while high-performance wired USB controllers can poll at 500 Hz to 1,000 Hz (1ms).

faq.q: How can I check if my thumbsticks have stick drift?
faq.a: Observe the Left and Right Stick radars when your fingers are completely off the thumbsticks. If the crosshair sits outside the center deadzone circle or coordinates display non-zero values, the potentiometer or Hall Effect sensor is exhibiting resting drift. Use our dedicated Gamepad Drift Visualizer for detailed circularity error profiling.

articleHtml:
Browser Gamepad Architecture and Input Normalization

The W3C Gamepad API provides direct access to physical gaming controllers via standard operating system Human Interface Device (HID) drivers. Understanding input mapping and analog stick telemetry ensures responsive, accurate control calibration.

The Standard Gamepad Button Mapping Specification

Controllers communicate across diverse hardware interfaces (USB HID, Microsoft XInput, and Bluetooth DirectInput). The W3C Gamepad specification establishes a normalized 17-button virtual topology:

  • Buttons 0 through 3 (Face Cluster): Normalized to Bottom, Right, Left, and Top primary actuation buttons (Cross/Circle/Square/Triangle or A/B/X/Y).
  • Buttons 4 and 5 (Bumpers): Digital shoulder switches L1/LB and R1/RB.
  • Buttons 6 and 7 (Triggers): Analog resistance triggers L2/LT and R2/RT delivering continuous floating-point pressure values from $0.00$ to $1.00$.
  • Axes 0 through 3 (Dual Thumbsticks): Two orthogonal Cartesian coordinates representing Left Stick ($X, Y$) and Right Stick ($X, Y$) within a $[-1.0, +1.0]$ range.

Analog Stick Deadzones and Potentiometer Wear

Traditional analog thumbsticks rely on dual carbon-film wiper potentiometers. As the spring centering mechanism wears mechanically over millions of cycles, the physical wiper may fail to return exactly to electrical zero $(0.000, 0.000)$. Game developers compensate by establishing software deadzones—typically between 5% and 12% circular radius:

$$\text{Stick Magnitude} = \sqrt{X^2 + Y^2}, \quad \text{In Deadzone if } \text{Magnitude} \le \text{Threshold}$$

Modern Hall Effect sensors substitute mechanical potentiometers with magnetic field induction sensors, effectively eliminating physical wiper friction and preventing potentiometer wear.
